group: Unit iv — Risk Assessment & Operational Safety
title: Risk in Degraded Operation, Failure Scenarios & Lessons Learned

questions.q: Degraded operation increases risk mainly because:
options: One or more automatic safety/operational barriers are unavailable, so humans must compensate
questions.explain: A lost automatic layer transfers its work to people — that transfer is the extra risk.

questions.q: A 'compensating barrier' in degraded working is:
options: An extra measure added to replace a lost barrier — lower speed, extra staff, Operations Control Centre (OCC) authorisation or time limits
A type of Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)
questions.explain: When a barrier is removed, compensating barriers are deliberately added so total protection is maintained.

questions.q: When Automatic Train Operation (ATO) fails and trains run in Automatic Train Protection (ATP) manual mode, a typical compensating measure is:
options: Reduced speed and increased headway as prescribed
questions.explain: A lost automatic layer is replaced by time, space and human attention.

questions.q: Automatic Train Protection (ATP) is isolated for a movement. The risk position is:
options: A routine matter needing nothing extra
A key functional barrier is gone — movement needs strict compensating controls and authorisation
questions.explain: Isolating Automatic Train Protection (ATP) removes the machine that stops the train — degraded rules and authorisation must fill the gap.

questions.q: One Platform Screen Door (PSD) door has failed and is isolated, with supervision posted. This is an example of:
options: Degraded working managed by a compensating measure (staff supervision)
questions.explain: A failed barrier plus a posted human compensating control is managed degraded working.

questions.q: Single-line working on a double-line section increases risk because:
options: A normal barrier — separate lines for each direction — is removed, so movements must be controlled by procedure and authorisation
questions.explain: Two-way traffic on one line survives on procedure: authorisation, communication and strict control.

questions.q: Which is NOT a compensating measure in degraded working?
options: Operations Control Centre (OCC) authorisation and time limits
Increasing speed to clear the section quickly
questions.explain: Speed is the enemy in degraded mode — compensations add time, people and control, never speed.

questions.q: Failure scenarios are studied in risk assessment so that:
options: Controls and responses are planned before the failure happens in service
questions.explain: Imagining the failure in advance is how the railway writes its degraded-working rules.

questions.q: After an incident, the investigation looks mainly for:
options: The root cause — why the barriers failed — not merely who was present
questions.explain: Root-cause investigation finds the failed layers; blame alone fixes nothing.

questions.q: 'Lessons learned' from an incident must lead to:
options: Blaming one person and closing the file
Changes in design, procedure or training, shared across the whole organisation
questions.explain: If the same failure can happen at the next station, the lesson was not learned.

questions.q: Corrective actions after an investigation are:
options: Tracked to closure, not just recommended
questions.explain: An action without follow-up is a wish. Tracking to closure is what makes it a control.

questions.q: Lessons are shared across the organisation through:
options: Word of mouth in one station
Circulars, training updates and rule changes
questions.explain: A lesson locked in one station's file protects nobody else; circulars and training spread it.

questions.q: Near-miss data prevents accidents because (Heinrich's principle):
options: Many near-misses precede one serious accident — fixing near-miss causes removes the accident's foundation
questions.explain: Near-misses are free lessons: the same causes, without the injury — yet.

questions.q: Which scenario is INTOLERABLE, where work must not start?
options: Staff on track with the Overhead Equipment (OHE) live and no possession
A wet platform with staff deployed
One Platform Screen Door (PSD) door isolated with supervision
questions.explain: Live Overhead Equipment (OHE) + people on track + no protection is the red zone of every risk matrix.

questions.q: In degraded working, why is extra communication required?
options: Because a procedural barrier must strengthen when automatic barriers weaken
questions.explain: Communication carries more of the safety load when machines carry less of it.

questions.q: Time limits on degraded working help because:
options: They bound the period of higher risk and force review or restoration
questions.explain: Degraded mode is a temporary state with an expiry — not a new normal.

questions.q: Scenario: Signalling fails on a section; trains are authorised by Operations Control Centre (OCC) at reduced speed with increased spacing. This is:
options: Degraded working with compensating barriers — authorisation, speed and spacing replacing the lost signalling layer
questions.explain: The pattern to recognise: lost barrier → named compensations → controlled continuation of service.

questions.q: What is the danger of degraded working continuing for a long time?
options: The temporary, higher-risk way of working starts to feel normal — normalisation of the degraded state
questions.explain: Degraded mode tolerated too long becomes an accepted risk — time limits and restoration pressure prevent that drift.

questions.q: An incident investigation that ends with 'driver error' and nothing else has failed because:
options: It has not asked why the system allowed one human error to become an accident — the root cause lies in the layers
questions.explain: Human error is the start of the question, not the end: which barriers should have caught it?

questions.q: Corrective and preventive actions differ in that corrective actions:
options: Happen only after the next accident
Fix the cause found, while preventive actions stop similar failures elsewhere before they happen
questions.explain: Fix here (corrective) and fix everywhere it could happen (preventive) — both come out of lessons learned.

questions.q: Scenario: A Platform Screen Door (PSD) fault repeats at three stations. 'Lessons learned' properly applied means:
options: Each station repairs its own quietly
A system-level fix — design/procedure change and a circular to all stations — not three local repairs
questions.explain: Repeated local failures are one system lesson. The fix and the message must travel organisation-wide.

questions.q: Why must lessons learned be written into rules and training?
options: So the protection survives staff transfers and time — the system remembers even when individuals forget
questions.explain: People rotate; rules and training are the organisation's memory.

questions.q: During degraded operation with a barrier removed, Operations Control Centre (OCC) authorisation is required because:
options: Drivers cannot be trusted at all
A senior, network-level decision must own the extra risk and set its conditions
questions.explain: Extra risk needs an owner: Operations Control Centre (OCC) authorises, sets speed/staff/time conditions and monitors the degraded state.

questions.q: A failure scenario in which several barriers fail together illustrates:
options: The Swiss-cheese model in real life — holes aligning across layers
questions.explain: Real accidents are multi-layer failures; that is why investigations examine every layer, not the last one only.

questions.q: What should happen to a compensating measure when normal working is restored?
options: It is withdrawn in order as the original barrier returns — degraded arrangements are formally closed
questions.explain: Degraded working is opened and closed formally; compensations end when the real barrier is back and proved.

questions.q: Incident prevention, as taught in this unit, is mainly built from:
options: Hazard identification, risk controls, barrier maintenance and lessons from past incidents and near-misses
questions.explain: Prevention is a system output: find hazards, control them, keep barriers alive and learn from every event.

questions.q: Scenario: After a near-miss, the enquiry finds a confusing procedure. The best lesson-learned action is:
options: Rewrite the procedure clearly, circulate it and train staff — and track the action to closure
Punish the staff who were confused
Wait for an accident to confirm
questions.explain: The procedure was a holed layer; fixing it, spreading it and verifying closure is the complete lesson cycle.

questions.q: Why are degraded-mode risks assessed separately from normal-mode risks?
options: Because the barrier set is different — risks that are controlled normally may be exposed when a layer is removed
questions.explain: Change the layers and you change the risk: degraded working needs its own assessment and controls.

questions.q: Extra staff posted during degraded working act as:
options: A human compensating barrier, watching and controlling what the failed system no longer does
questions.explain: People replace the machine's eyes and hands — that is a deliberate barrier substitution, with its own limits.

questions.q: The final test of whether a lesson was truly learned is:
options: The same failure does not happen again — because design, procedure or training actually changed
A circular was printed but unread
questions.explain: Learning is proved by changed reality, not by paperwork.

questions.q: A common-cause failure is dangerous in degraded operation because:
options: It is very rare and can be ignored
One single event — such as a total power failure — can disable several barriers at the same time, exactly when the operation is already weakened
It only affects one small component
questions.explain: Normal safety assumes barriers fail one at a time. A common cause — power, flooding, a shared system — knocks out several together, which is why degraded modes demand fresh assessment instead of business as usual.

questions.q: 'Normalisation of deviance' — a known accident precursor — means:
options: Small rule deviations are repeated without an accident, so the deviation slowly starts to be treated as normal and acceptable, until the day conditions align for a disaster
questions.explain: Every shortcut that 'worked last time' teaches the team the wrong lesson. Investigations of major accidents repeatedly find that the fatal practice had become routine long before the accident — the deviance had been normalised.

questions.q: A 'lesson learned' from an incident is genuinely learned only when:
options: It is mentioned in a meeting
It results in an actual change — to procedure, training, design or supervision — and the change is verified to be in use
It is written in a report that is filed
questions.explain: A lesson identified is not a lesson learned. Learning is complete only when something in the real system changes and someone checks that the change is actually being followed on the ground.

questions.q: Degraded working that continues for many hours without restoration creates extra risk mainly through:
options: Staff fatigue, growing workarounds and fading vigilance — the longer the abnormal state lasts, the more its own hazards grow
questions.explain: Degraded mode is a bridge, not a destination. Time pressure, tired staff and improvised practices accumulate, so the plan must either restore normal working or step the service down to a level the degraded state can safely sustain.

questions.q: Contingency plans for failures are exercised through drills and simulations mainly so that:
options: Staff can be marked for promotion
Staff discover the plan's gaps and build real skill in safety, instead of reading the plan for the first time during a real emergency
questions.explain: A plan that has never been practised is a hope, not a capability. Drills expose missing equipment, unclear roles and slow steps while the cost of finding them is still zero.
